1#א: The seller. Shach wrote: even an Israelite established in kashrut who says they are from such-and-such fowl and we recognize that that fowl is pure — we do not rely on him; and even if he shows us the fowl and says the eggs come from it he is not believed, for he certainly lies.
1#ב: Relies. The reason: when he says it is from such-and-such fowl it is a presumption he does not lie because he fears lest they bring eggs of that fowl and they see they do not resemble these and he is shamed; and Taz wrote there is no room to say that since there are raven eggs resembling dove eggs he could evade and say they are dove eggs; nevertheless he fears lest an Israelite set his mind on them that there cannot fail to be some difference between them.
1#ג: Not. The reason: when they bring eggs of a pure fowl and they do not resemble them, he can say: I did not tell you these are from this fowl but from another fowl you do not recognize, and it is pure.
1#ד: Tereifah. For most eggs are kosher; and Shach wrote that according to the Rav in his hagahah, even without recognizable familiarity we rely on him when he says they are from such-and-such fowl and we recognize that it is pure.
2#_: In signs. Taz wrote: even if a non-Jewess brought and broke them before us unintentionally and we had not yet recognized by familiarity that they are chicken eggs — nevertheless permitted and we rely on the majority; except where the non-Jew explicitly says they are from an uncommon species — then signs are required. And Shach wrote in name of a sage that the custom is to buy bar-goose eggs called enten, some in white shells and some in green shells, because they recognize in them that they are bar-goose eggs whose way is thus.
3#א: Nevelah. Shach wrote: an egg of nevelah is forbidden only d'rabbanan, for from the Torah it is permitted, for it is impossible it should be completed after death; but an egg of tereifah is forbidden from the Torah because afterward it was completed in prohibition, and even if it became tereifah only near shechitah it is forbidden from the Torah (they do not distinguish) — see above end of seif 99 and end of siman 87 seif 5.
3#ב: In a thousand. This applies also to an egg of nevelah, for since it is an egg of nevelah the prohibition is certainly established and it is not nullified; unlike when it is a doubt of an egg of nevelah which is a rabbinic doubt and lenient. But in a doubt of an egg of tereifah, which is d'oraisa, they were stringent. However, it requires study according to what Mechaber and Rama ruled in siman 110 that it should nullify in a majority — dry in dry, one in two is nullified — and specifically an egg that has a chick in it is a complete creature, but an ordinary egg is not. And it requires study.
3#ג: Permitted. For it is a rabbinic doubt; and even if we know certainly from which chicken it is, only that there is doubt whether the chicken is nevelah or slaughtered — such as doubt in shechitah where the halachah is it is invalid — the egg is permitted.
5#א: Peeled. Shach wrote: it appears that even though the others are also in their shells it is forbidden until sixty-one, and the shell of the permitted combines — by way of example: if there are fifty permitted eggs and the shells hold ten eggs, that is insufficient but sixty-one are required (the reason is that peeled is the power of fire dominating it and extracting the body of the prohibition, and it is like an egg that has a chick in it which forbids even if not peeled — Taz, and Shach agreed). And not like Bach who is lenient if the forbidden is peeled and the permitted is not peeled and permits everything — this does not seem correct at all; see there.
5#ב: Sixty-one. The reason: many poskim wrote that because there are large and small eggs they therefore added one; and for this reason when it was cooked in a permitted dish one needs only sixty of the dish to nullify it — this is Mechaber's view; but Rambam wrote the reason is because it is a complete creature in itself they made a distinction and added to its measure; and for this reason even in a dish one needs sixty-one to nullify; however for this reason if it became tereifah in a bowl one needs only sixty; and according to Mechaber one needs sixty-one — and one should be stringent for both reasons, end of his words.
5#ג: Chick. The reason is that the meat is forbidden; and the same applies to blood found in it — a drop of blood that spreads through all of it, as above siman 66, and it is considered as if there is a chick in it — specifically when it is known the blood is in the place that forbids it; but in a doubt of mixtures it is permitted as in siman 66.
5#ד: Siman 99. Meaning: there it was explained that where there is no great loss one may not combine bones of prohibition to nullify — and the same applies here; and Taz distinguishes that specifically in a dish the shell of prohibition combines with the permitted, but not with ordinary eggs — sixty-one are required to nullify it.
7#א: Permitted. The reason is stated in the Gemara and poskim: because the chick is not formed from the egg until after it spoils, and it is like mere dust.
7#ב: And some say. Shach wrote: and Taz omitted this entire hagahah and rightly intended — why should we be stringent in something found explicitly permitted in the Gemara and all poskim; and Taz wrote the reason one should be concerned lest he keep it in his house under the chicken to make a chick from it and it will be permitted, and there is concern for mishap lest meanwhile he eat it — as we find this matter stated explicitly in Mishnah chapter 8 of Terumot, that for this reason they decreed that growths of terumah too are terumah, lest he keep impure terumah until sowing time — and it requires study to resolve this in the Gemara, end of his words. And Nekudot HaKesef challenged this — some say for terumah which is common; see there.
8#_: Rebelliousness. Perishah challenged: for in siman 66 Tur wrote that if it is known the chick is formed they are liable on it from the Torah; and he resolved: there, blood is found inside the egg — therefore forbidden from the Torah because of blood; unlike here where the blood already turned and became clotted and is dust and has no d'oraisa prohibition; and Taz in siman 66 resolved: here it speaks where there is no blood, only formation of flesh — and this is d'rabbanan, end of his words.
9#א: We wait. Taz wrote: some say to what Rama wrote in siman 57 that we are concerned for mishap even in a doubt of tereifah — there it is different because one must wait twelve months; but here the time is short. But in Beit Yosef he wrote: even regarding fowl one does not wait except a day — immediately one slaughters and sells to a non-Jew, meaning sells to a non-Jew and the non-Jew slaughters afterward — see above siman 57.
9#ב: Doubt. Shach wrote: but certainly tereifah — no; and see siman 57 and siman 81.
10#א: In what case is this said. That it is forbidden to buy from a non-Jew.
10#ב: They practice. And a sage wrote: nevertheless one should not buy cracked eggs from a non-Jew; see there. And Shach wrote: however, it may be that these poskim who permit speak of a non-Jew who is not signed; but a non-Jew who is commonly signed often mixes with bread — cracked eggs — and we are concerned lest he sell to an Israelite, end of his words.
